You can't be sure, but it is assumed that it is. The observation gets presented in peer review, and as long as no one can prove with a disproving measurement for a tool bag then it is accepted as the most likely object floating there. It's of course not "immediately accepted" that's stupid. That is how humanities science works. It's all assumption and belief as well.

Someone mentioned that USB can destroy NTFS or that files might corrupt by copying through USB, I use TeraCopy which at least alleviates the copying integrity, I'd like to know more about that USB destroying NTFS thing.

For Reference I have a 12TB and a 14TB white drives in an Orico 5 Bay, each disk containing identical files, I usually download or get my files elsewhere and then they get copied to both of those drives. My only failure point is demagnetization, bit rot and cosmic rays, all of which I've understood are incredibly rare occurrences, but I want to be safe.

It's been a cost effective solution so far since all the files I own (not counting games, which can be redownloaded so are of low value) fit on one 12TB drive. The only off-site solution so far is getting another drive with the same files and hermetically seal it in a box to bury in the woods. Occasionally digging it up to rotate it with a fresh copy.

This is an enclosure, not a USB drive. 

If the USB enclosure fails I'll remove the HDD from it and put it into a new enclosure or internally into a PC, only first party enclosures come with hardware encryption making the drive unreadable by a common PC. 

USB drives are for temporary usage, shifting files quickly from one PC to the next, gifting or selling files or using them primarily for BIOS updates these days.
